name: GFT: November Edition in Vasant Vihar
description: Grounds for Thought: Vasant Vihar, November 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Thursday evenings. Three very different conversations.12th November: Palak ChananaLove Actually? Attachment Styles, Situationships & the Patterns We Keep Repeating. Why do you keep finding the same kind of person? Why is it so hard to say what you need, or to leave when you meant to, or to stop repeating a pattern you thought you'd already moved past? Palak Chanana, a counselling psychologist and neuro-queer affirmative therapist who founded UnTangle Yourself, draws on anonymised, composite themes from individual and couples counselling to explore how fear, expectation, and past experience quietly shape the way we connect. This isn't a session about finding the right partner or following relationship rules — it's an invitation to get curious about how you love, what you actually need, and what you keep repeating without noticing.19th November: Deborishi GogoiVisceral Pleasures of Viewing Horror Cinema You're gripping your pillow, heart racing, yelling "don't go in there" — and loving every second of it. For decades, film theory explained this through Freud: repression, the unconscious, hidden anxiety. Deborishi Gogoi, a PhD scholar at Shiv Nadar Institution of Eminence working on folk horror and the critique of ideology, argues that account misses the most important part — what watching horror actually feels like, moment by moment, in the body. Through the framing, sound, and editing rhythm of three recent horror films — Suspiria, Midsommar, and The Ugly Stepsister — this session builds the case that horror's pleasure isn't saved for the ending. It's built into the dread itself.26th November: Vasundhara BhojvaidBreathing Delhi: Can a City Hold Air? What does it mean to live in a city where the atmosphere itself feels like confinement? Vasundhara Bhojvaid, Associate Professor of Sociology at Shiv Nadar University, works with a concept she calls "Hawa-laat" — a play on hawalaat, a police lockup, and the physical jolt of Delhi's toxic air. Moving past ecological data into what she calls our "aerial imaginations," this session asks how an invisible hazard like air pollution quietly reconfigures relationships, redraws urban space, and reshapes what survival means in a city that can no longer take its air for granted.

name: Clearing the Smoke and Mirrors
description: In late October, Mumbai's AQI crossed 320 while Delhi sat at 176, its cleanest reading for that date in a decade. So what does it mean when the capital is breathing easier than the coast?Not much, if you ask the people who study this. A single day's AQI is a weather report as much as a pollution report, and one clean week in Delhi is not a solved problem any more than one bad week in Mumbai is a new one. But the comparison is useful, because it puts pressure on the assumption most of us carry around: that this is a Delhi problem, caused by Delhi things, fixable by Delhi alone.We've all done the winter ritual. Complaining about the AQI, feeling what the air does to our lungs, sleep, skin and routines. Every year we're handed the same list of culprits: stubble burning, construction dust, industrial emissions, cars, trucks, garbage fires, landfills, brick kilns, diesel generators and, of course, the wind. The panels shout, the season passes, and by next November we're no clearer on which of these actually matters, or by how much.Atmospheric scientist Dr Mohammad Rafiuddin starts with the hand Delhi has been dealt: a landlocked city on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, hemmed in by the Himalayas, with winter air that sits still. It's a bad hand, but not a unique one, and if cities elsewhere with the same conditions have got their air under control, so can this one. From there we go sector by sector through what is actually in the air we breathe, which sources genuinely move the needle, and why the answer never stops at Delhi's border.The session explores:Why a daily AQI number tells you as much about the weather as about pollutionHow Delhi's geography and winter stillness trap what we put into the air, and why that isn't an excuseWhat's actually in the air, sector by sector: transport, biomass and solid-fuel burning, waste, dust, construction, industry and stubbleWhich sources matter most, by how much, and which solutions would genuinely cut emissions from eachAbout the SpeakerDr Mohammad Rafiuddin is an atmospheric scientist who once built a fog-forecasting system for Bengaluru airport, which means pilots have landed on his maths. He is now Programme Lead – Clean Air at CEEW, where he researches what Delhi's air is made of, how well the city can predict it, and why the answer never stops at Delhi's border. He holds a PhD in atmospheric sciences from the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru, a Post Graduate Diploma in Urban Environmental Management and Law from National Law University, and a BTech in mechanical engineering from Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Hyderabad.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. description: Beyond the crowded bazaars and familiar landmarks of Old Delhi lies a carefully layered historic city shaped by faith, community, poetry and a distinctive way of urban life. The walk also examines the design of traditional havelis and the architectural principles that created private worlds behind their seemingly modest street-facing entrances.From the remarkable legacy of Digambar Jain Lal Mandir and Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib to the hidden heritage of Naughara and the enduring presence of Fatehpuri Masjid, the walk reveals how different communities shaped the city. A visit to Ghalib ki Haveli adds another layer, connecting Shahjahanabad's streets with the literary and cultural world of nineteenth-century Delhi.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Shahjahanabad as a planned Mughal city and an exploration of how its streets, markets and neighbourhoods developed around communities, occupations, faith and everyday life.Visit Digambar Jain Lal Mandir and explore the remarkable legacy of Delhi's oldest Jain temple while understanding the relationship between sacred spaces and the surrounding urban neighbourhood.Continue to Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib and uncover its powerful story of faith, sacrifice and resilience within the historic landscape of Chandni Chowk.Walk through the historic streets and neighbourhoods of Shahjahanabad while understanding the difference between a kucha, katra and gali, and how these spaces shaped movement, trade, privacy and community life.Explore Naughara and discover its hidden Jain temples and beautifully preserved heritage havelis.Understand how traditional havelis were designed, from their relationship with the street to the organisation of private and shared spaces within, and examine how architecture responded to the social life of the city.Continue through the hidden streets of Chandni Chowk, discovering architectural details and neighbourhood stories that reveal how Shahjahanabad functioned as a living city.Visit Ghalib ki Haveli and step into the literary world of Mirza Ghalib, exploring poetry, culture and everyday life in nineteenth-century Delhi.Visit Fatehpuri Masjid and understand its significance within the urban and commercial landscape of Shahjahanabad.Conclude with a discussion on how faith, communities, neighbourhood planning and architecture came together to create one of India's most remarkable living historic cities.

description: Grounds for Thought: Mehrauli, November 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought brings researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into rooms full of curious people, where the conversation goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This November in Delhi moves from the hidden mathematics behind everyday intuitions to modern love, from caste and labour to the pleasures of horror cinema, from AI at the margins to the air Delhi breathes.3rd November: Awanish Pandey Is a Second Medical Opinion Always Reliable? The Hidden Maths Behind Every Decision Why does food at an expensive restaurant sometimes taste worse than food at a roadside dhaba? Why are the most attractive celebrities rarely the most talented, and vice versa? Awanish Pandey, Assistant Professor at IIT Delhi's Optics and Photonics Centre and a former researcher at CERN, argues that questions like these are already mathematics in disguise — and that some of our strongest intuitions about the world are built on nothing sturdier than a convincing pattern. No equations, no background required: just curiosity, and a healthy suspicion of things that seem obvious.17th November: Moggallan BhartiHow Does Caste Haunt the Dreams of Modern India and Its Workers? Caste in India doesn't stay confined to its "seemingly societal concerns" — it shapes who gets to labour, how that labour is valued, and what social standing comes attached to it. Moggallan Bharti, Assistant Professor at Ambedkar University's School of Development Studies and a researcher of Dalit politics, argues that the labour theory of value cannot be understood in India apart from the caste structure it's embedded in. name: The Criminal Profiling Masterclass
description: Inside a Profiler's Mind: Four Sessions on Criminal ProfilingThink like a profiler. Reason like a scientist.You've probably watched the shows. The detective looks at a crime scene for a few seconds, pauses, and describes the killer right down to his childhood. It's great TV, but is it how profiling actually works?Across four sessions, criminologist and forensic psychologist Rithin Joseph separates movie myth from method. We go from 19th-century attempts to spot criminals by the shape of their skulls, to the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, to the maths of where offenders live, to how profiling is actually done in 2026. Every session digs into real true crime cases, runs its own hands-on simulation, and has much more along the way, so you won't just be listening. You'll be profiling.Each session stands on its own, so come to one or come to all four. Book all four and get a discount, for anyone who wants the full case file.21st November, 12–2 PM: Can You Tell If I'm a Serial Killer?Profiling's real history is messier than the legend, and much more interesting. We start with Lombroso and phrenology, who believed you could read criminality in someone's face, and look at why those ideas caught on and why they fell apart. Then we follow Hans Gross's turn toward evidence, James Brussel's famous (and contested) Mad Bomber profile, and the rise of the FBI's behavioural analysts. Along the way we ask what profiling can actually tell an investigator, and what it never can.22nd November, 12–2 PM: Same Crime, Different Profiles: Who Gets It Right?Two profilers look at the same crime scene and come back with two different suspects. How does that happen? This session gets into the reasoning behind profiling: patterns drawn from many offenders versus clues taken from one case, and the FBI's famous split between "organised" and "disorganised" offenders, with cases like BTK and Jeffrey Dahmer as reference points. We'll look at where that split helps and where it falls apart, and at the biases that slip in without anyone noticing. Then we'll test ourselves on a fictional scene that has two competing profiles.28th November, 3–5 PM: Where Do Killers Live? The Geography of CrimeA series of crimes leaves more than physical evidence. It leaves a map. Using David Canter's investigative psychology and Kim Rossmo's geographic profiling, we'll look at how offenders move through a city: comfort zones, anchor points, and why distance matters. The DC Sniper case runs through the session. Then we'll take a fictional cluster of crime locations and try to narrow the search ourselves. A warning in advance: these maps deal in probabilities, not GPS coordinates.29th November, 3–5 PM: What Criminal Profiling Looks Like in 2026Instead of asking "what kind of person would do this?", modern profiling asks "what does the evidence actually show?" This session introduces Behavioral Evidence Analysis, which reads the crime scene, the victim's circumstances and the sequence of events before it reaches for any stereotype. We'll work out the difference between how a crime was committed and what it might reveal about the person behind it. Then we'll read a fictional case file twice and watch our conclusions change as new evidence comes in.All sessions at the Gully Labs store, Panchsheel Park.About the speakerRithin Joseph is an Assistant Professor at the School of Behavioural Forensics, National Forensic Sciences University, Delhi, where he teaches criminology and forensic psychology. He is certified in investigative tools including the polygraph, BEOS brain profiling, Layered Voice Analysis and EyeDetect. He is Co-Investigator on an ICSSR-funded study predicting recidivism among first-time offenders, co-author of Crime as the Cause of Criminality and BRICS: Unravelling the Abyss, and a gold medallist in his Master's in Criminology.Four sessions, four case files, and you'll never watch a crime show the same way again.

name: K se Karuna: India’s Intellectual Inheritance
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that asks where our political vocabulary, that we use almost every day - actually came from:Liberty, equality, fraternity. Three words that built the modern nation, and all three arrived here from somewhere else. What if the organising idea had come from within South Asia instead?The nation-making of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries settled on that trio, and we have lived inside it ever since: in constitutional safeguards, in the language of rights, in what we understand democratic life to guarantee. Ideas that germinated in the continental world and travelled into the Global South as imports, carrying both a formal-legal meaning and a substantive promise for how people might live together.Pia David turns to a different inheritance. Karuṇā, compassion, is an idea that emerges from within this geography, and it has its own long history of thinking about difference, diversity and ethical living. Not only in the ancient past, but through the reformist and political thought of modern India, where it kept resurfacing in arguments about what a shared life demands.The question the lecture leaves us with is a live one. What would it mean to treat karuṇā not as sentiment but as political method?A way of addressing global conflict, human despair, and the particular poverty that enters political discourse when compassion goes missing from it?The session explores:How liberty, equality and fraternity became the default grammar of modern political lifeKaruṇā as an idea with its own intellectual lineage in South Asia, ancient and modernHow questions of diversity, difference and ethical living were imagined from within this regionWhat compassion offers as a mode of praxis, not just a normative horizon for theory, but something politics could actually doAbout the SpeakerPia David is from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, and is trained as a political scientist. As a Foundation for Universal Responsibility Dalai Lama Studies Fellow in 2023, she worked on Dharma and Dhamma: A Modern Reading of Gandhi and Ambedkar in the Context of Deep Diversity. Her interests span liberal political philosophy and social and political thought from South Asia in the context of the world. She can be found on long walks through forested gardens, tombs and ruins, usually with friends, sometimes in solitude, never without music. Her current favourite is Libertango. She lives in Delhi, wondering about Mir's lament on his exile.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Who Does the City Belong To?
description: Who Does the City Belong To?A conversation on public space and the lawYou have probably stood in front of a barricade this year. A road closed with no notice. A park gate locked at night. A station shut, a lane that used to be a shortcut now ending in a guard and a boom. Most of us have learned to route around it without thinking.But there’s a question underneath that almost none of us can answer: what are we actually entitled to in a public space and what happens when that space is closed, fenced or policed?In this edition of The Human City Conversations, we’ll ask what the Constitution actually gives us by way of a right to assemble and to protest. Whether a government can simply take a Jantar Mantar away. Whether there is such a thing as a right to walk in an Indian city, and who in Delhi really has it. And how much of what we call planning is in truth a question of who is expected to justify their presence in public, and who is not.It isn’t a lecture, and it isn’t a complaint session. It’s an hour of conversation, in plain words, followed by your questions put directly to someone who has spent two decades arguing these things in court.About the guestMihira Sood is a lawyer and scholar in the field of women’s rights, and practices at the Supreme Court of India and the Delhi High Court. She has taught at Jindal Global Law School and National Law University Delhi, and holds degrees from NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and Columbia Law School, New York. She was among the youngest members to assist the Justice Verma Committee, whose recommendations reshaped India’s criminal law on sexual violence. She writes and speaks widely on women’s rights, feminist jurisprudence, equality law and civil liberties, and is a regular commentator in the national press. She has recently written a book Courting Equality which focusses on the Landmark Cases in the Battle for Women’s Rights (Juggernaut) traces fifty years of the law’s encounter with women’s lives — from the anti-dowry agitations of the 1970s, through Shah Bano and the Uniform Civil Code debate, to the Nirbhaya movement and its continuing reverberations, and on to the present backlash against the supposed misuse of these very laws.Copies will be on sale at Kunzum on the evening, at 20% off.About the seriesThe Human City Conversations is the live edition of The Human City Podcast, hosted by Ruchita Bansal, which for the past year has asked how Indian cities are planned, built and experienced — and who they are built for. description: At the Safer Internet India coalition, our focus has always been on keeping the safety of every internet user at the centre of the conversation. As more of our lives move online, from how we learn and work to how we bank and connect, trust has become the foundation that a safer internet is built on.With that in mind, we are pleased to announce the theme for the Safer Internet India Summit 2027: “Making Trust Matter”.Join us on 9 February 2027, Safer Internet Day, as we bring together voices from industry, government, academia and civil society to discuss youth safety, the future of online safety, and the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead.

location.address: New Delhi, Delhi, India
